paragraphs:
Nevula. Rashi, Bava Metzia, Eizehu Neshekh 67a, explains 'you and nevula' as 'you and he.' I do not know who told him this was a sage. Rashi there, citing geonic responsa, explains that venula is Aramaic, used of male or female when wishing to say 'you and he' or 'you and she'; 'but I say this is her name.' End of quotation. Either way it is a woman's name, as the passage says: a woman told a man to buy land from her relative; he bought it for her. The relative asked the intermediary, 'If I had money, would you return the land to me?' The intermediary replied, 'You and Nevula are kin.' How then did Yuḥasin include it among sages' names?

I saw Asifat Zekenim, Bava Metzia there, quoting R. Tzemaḥ bar Paltoi Gaon's responsum: 'You and nula are siblings'—he told her, 'He is your relative; you and nula,' you and he. Likewise HaMappelt 25: they taught in our teachers' name that they testified a sandal must have a face's form. R. Bivi said: R. Yoḥanan said this mishnah was taught from R. Neḥunya's testimony. R. Zeira said Rav Bivi merited this teaching: 'I and nevula sat before R. Yoḥanan when he stated it, and he preceded me and said it' (see Rav Bivi bar Avin). 'I and nevula' means only I and he. Likewise Mi SheAḥazo: one day 'he and nevula' sat in the house—only Shelomoh and Ashmedai—and Shelomoh told Ashmedai, 'It is written, like the might of the wild ox to him,' etc.: these are ministering angels. Up to here in §של״ע [as printed here; Shita Mekubetzet reads §339]. End of quotation. Thus nevula apparently means 'he'; so Rashi seems to explain. Why then did Yuḥasin include it? Perhaps he thought Niyuli (see his entry) was a sage's name.
